data.name: Guide_Title
data.value: Rules for writing a Chickxel script effect

data.name: Guide_Intro
data.value: Chickxel is a pixel-art editor. A script effect is one small JavaScript source that changes a layer's image for each frame. Follow the rules below; an effect that breaks them can't be read or is skipped for that frame. Only the names in the API list below are available.

data.name: Guide_RulesHeading
data.value: Rules

data.name: Guide_RuleOneFile
data.value: Write one complete JavaScript source. Call `effect({ ... })` exactly once at the top level; besides it, use only `const` values and `function` declarations (no import, export or modules).

data.name: Guide_RuleDeclaration
data.value: `name` (the effect name, 1-{nameMax} characters) is required. Always also write `description` (one short sentence about the effect, up to {descriptionMax} characters) and `tags` (3-6 lowercase English tags people would search for, e.g. `tags: ["neon", "glow", "outline"]`: lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, no repeats). Publishing uses this description and these tags as they are. Also write a `previewChick` sample that shows the effect well (one of: {chicks}). An effect that draws on its own without a chick, such as rain or snow, uses `previewChick: "none"` to be shown on an empty canvas. For a moving effect, `previewFrames` ({framesMin}-{framesMax}, default {framesDefault}) sets how many preview frames show one cycle.

data.name: Guide_RuleRender
data.value: `render(img, ctx, s)` changes `img.data` (RGBA 0-255, row by row; the red of pixel (x, y) is at `(y * img.width + x) * 4`) in place and returns nothing. Usually skip transparent pixels (alpha 0).

data.name: Guide_RuleDeterministic
data.value: The same image, frame and settings must always give the same result. `Date`, `Math.random` (use `ctx.hash(x, y, seed, salt?)` or `ctx.random(seed)` instead), `eval`/`Function`, files, network, timers and console are not available.

data.name: Guide_RuleRandom
data.value: When randomness fits the effect (explosions, debris, particles, sparks, dust, glitches, scattered pixels, jitter), use it freely so it looks natural, but always through the seeded `ctx.hash(x, y, seed, salt)` or `ctx.random(seed)`. Add a seed setting `{ key: "seed", label: "Seed", type: "int", min: 0, max: 9999, default: 1 }` (keep the key `seed`: the effects window then shows a dice button beside it that picks another seed) and pass `s.seed`, so every seed gives a different pattern and the same seed always looks the same. Give each random quantity its own salt (e.g. 0 = direction, 1 = speed, 2 = size) and key it by something stable such as the particle index or the source pixel or cell position, not by loop order, so a particle keeps the same path on every frame. Feed `ctx.step` or the frame in only for values that should change per frame (flicker, glitch).

data.name: Guide_RuleLimits
data.value: Limits per frame: {seconds} s, {statements} statements, {megabytes} MB of allocations, plus {pixelStatements} statements, {pixelMicroseconds} µs and {pixelKilobytes} KB for every pixel of the image, so larger images get proportionally more. Over a limit the effect is skipped for that frame. Keep the work proportional to the pixel count (no big loop per pixel).

data.name: Guide_RuleSettings
data.value: Put values the user can change in `settings: [{ key, label, type, ... }]`. type is `int` or `number` (min, max, step, default), `bool` (default), `color` (default "#RRGGBB"), `choice` (choices: [{ value, label }], default is one value), `colorList` (min/max items, default ["#RRGGBB", ...]), `colorPairs` (default [{ from: "#RRGGBB", to: "#RRGGBB" }, ...]) or `layer` (the user picks one of the document's layers; default is a layer name such as "ground", omit it for none). Read them in render as `s.key` (for colors see the gradient rule below, for layers the layer rule). When a setting only matters for some value of another setting, show it only then with `when`: `when: { facing: "rotate" }` (a value of an earlier `choice` setting; several values as `["rotate", "flip"]`) or `when: { closePath: true }` (an earlier `bool` setting). With several conditions all must match; a hidden setting keeps its value and is still readable as `s.key`.

data.name: Guide_RuleUsefulSettings
data.value: Before writing, decide on your own which settings make the effect useful and add them without being asked. Think first about where the effect is anchored: around the pivot (`ctx.pivot`), the center (`ctx.center`) or the source's bounds (`ctx.source`) — offer a `choice` when more than one makes sense. Then consider direction, speed and easing, loop / ping-pong / repeat count, start and end of the range, offsets, colors (the user can turn them into gradients), intensity and size, and for an effect that reads another layer a `layer` setting. Keep them purposeful (usually 3-8) with defaults that look good on the preview chick.

data.name: Guide_RuleGradient
data.value: The user can switch any color setting (`color`, and the items of `colorList` and `colorPairs`) from a solid color to a gradient in the effects window. So when you use a color, it is best to pick it at every pixel you write with `ctx.color("key", x, y)` (lists: `ctx.colorAt("key", i, x, y)`, pairs: `ctx.pairColor("key", i, "to", x, y)`) instead of reading `s.key` once, so a gradient shows as a natural per-pixel variation. String-literal keys keep the fast path. The gradient spans the opaque bounds of the image before the effect by default; when that doesn't fit the shape, pass bounds `{ x, y, w, h }` as the last argument (e.g. a beam's own rectangle or a ring's bounds). Keep a flat `s.key` color only when the effect really needs one solid color. Example: less good: `const c = s.glow;` read once outside the loop, then `d[i] = c.r;` / good: inside the pixel loop, `const c = ctx.color("glow", x, y); d[i] = c.r;`. The Effect Maker check lists color settings that stay one flat color with a gradient (a recommendation, not an error).

data.name: Guide_RuleAnimated
data.value: If the look changes over time, write `animated: true` and use `ctx.progress` (0-1 over the effect's range) or `ctx.t`. A still effect must look the same on every frame. Effects that spread outside the layer (glow, shadow, shake) make room with `padding`. When the user confirms the effects window, the canvas grows to fit what an effect draws past it (each effect can turn this off); for an effect that should be cut off by the canvas instead of growing it (like flames rising above the picture), declare `expandCanvas: false` so it starts off.

data.name: Guide_RuleMovePivot
data.value: If your effect moves/translates the subject (shake, bob, jump, throw, slide-in…), report that offset every frame inside `render` with `ctx.movePivot(dx, dy)` (pixels, image-coordinate directions, same units as `ctx.pivot`) so later effects in the list that work around the pivot (rotation, squash, scale) follow the moved subject, and the app widens the drawing area by that distance so a subject moved past `padding` is not cut off (without the call it is). Frames that do not move (0, 0) need no call; the user can turn this off per effect. To add the effect with it off, declare `movePivot: false`.

data.name: Guide_RuleFast
data.value: To run fast, keep render to numbers and booleans: `let`/`const` numbers, loops, `if`, `Math`, `lerp`, helper functions taking numbers, and reading and writing `img.data`. Strings, objects, arrays, closures, recursion, or assigning to anything other than `let` numbers and `img.data` make it run on the slower Jint interpreter (same result, slower). The Effect Maker shows which path runs and why.

data.name: Guide_RuleLayers
data.value: To read or act on another layer, add a `layer` setting (e.g. `{{ key: "target", label: "…", type: "layer", default: "ground" }}`) so the user picks the layer from the document's layers, and read it with `ctx.layer("target")` (its image without effects), `ctx.layerWithEffects("target")` (with its effects) or `ctx.layerEffects("target")` (names of its effects). Layers can't be read by position or by a name written in the code. These functions only see layers inside a project (null elsewhere) and automatically add the tag `{tag}`. `ctx.layer` and `ctx.layerWithEffects` stay on the fast path when the key is written as a string literal and you check the result with `if (!g)`, `g ? … : …` or `g === null` before reading `g.data` / `g.width` (`const gd = g ? g.data : null` is fine too); `ctx.layerEffects` runs on Jint. In the Effect Maker each effect has a preview scene (extra layers around the chick, edited in the main editor) whose layers the setting lists: use a scene layer's name as the default. They return null (or an empty array) when nothing is chosen or the layer is missing: always handle that gracefully, e.g. by drawing the effect without it.

data.name: Guide_RuleFrames
data.value: Effects that use other frames' images (a morph that turns one image into another, afterimages and so on) read frame i's image before effects with `ctx.frameSource(i)` (null if there is none or its size differs, so always check). The effect range's first and last frame numbers are `ctx.rangeStart` and `ctx.rangeEnd`, and the name of the frame tag the current frame is in is `ctx.frameTag` ("" if none). To move the pixels of two images onto each other, pair them with `ctx.matchPixels(a, b)` (by position; pass `"color"` as the third argument to pair by color) and draw each pair `[ax, ay, bx, by]` of the returned `data` along `ctx.progress` (clear `img.data` first and blend each pair's colors read from a and b at those spots). Effects that call `ctx.frameSource` also draw on frames without a cel (on a blank image), so a morph only needs images on its first and last frames. For a morph, set `previewEndChick` in the declaration to an end chick: the preview's last frame then shows that chick and `ctx.frameSource(ctx.rangeEnd)` reads it. When the effect matters most if the two images sit in different places or have different centers, also declare `previewEndOffset: [x, y]` (moves the end chick) and `previewPivot` / `previewEndPivot: [x, y]` (moves `ctx.pivot` of the other frames / the last frame from the chick's center; px, each -64 to 64) to show it in the preview. Effects that read other frames automatically get the tag `{tag}`. The preview chick stays in place unless `previewMotion` is declared, so effects that react to movement (afterimages, trails) declare `previewMotion: "right"` (or `"left"`, `"up"`, `"down"`: 1 px per frame, or `[[x, y], ...]` with one place per frame) to show in the preview.

data.name: Guide_RuleLanguage
data.value: Write the name, description, setting labels and choice labels in the user's language (`tags` are always English), and always set `language` to the code of that language (e.g. `language: "en"`, `"ko"`, `"ja"`, `"zh-Hans"`). If you rewrite the declared name, description or labels in another language, change `language` too. If the user's language is not English, always also write `translations.en` with an English `name`, `description` and `labels` for every setting and choice (`labels: { key: "…", "key.choiceValue": "…" }`). Whenever you change the effect, check that `description` and `tags` still fit it and update them; whenever you change the name, description, settings or choices, update `translations.en` and every other existing translation to match.

data.name: Guide_AnswerHeading
data.value: Answer format

data.name: Guide_Answer
data.value: Answer with one complete JavaScript file in a single code block (opened with three backticks and js) (from start to end, not only the changed part or fragments), followed by at most a few sentences. The user pastes the whole block into the Effect Maker editor.

data.name: Guide_SourceHeading
data.value: Current source

data.name: Guide_SourceNote
data.value: The source the user is editing in the Effect Maker. If asked for a change, start from this source.

data.name: Guide_RuleClipping
data.value: When the user turns on "Clip to effect above" for an effect in the effects window, `img` holds only the pixels drawn by the nearest non-clipped effect above it (everything else transparent), and the result is laid over the picture even where it spreads outside those pixels (flames clipped to a rain effect grow from the raindrops). So an effect meant to grow from another effect's result just draws from the visible pixels of `img`; nothing has to be declared for clipping (the old `clipsBySource` and `erasesSource` are ignored).
